name: Energy medicine

card.summary: A group of healing practices, such as Reiki and biofield therapy, based on the belief that a body energy field can be balanced; people use it for relaxation and stress relief that some link to how they look.
card.note: Reviews report no evidence of clinical efficacy; harm arises mainly when it replaces medical treatment.

quick.overview:
Energy medicine covers practices in which healers claim to channel or rebalance a body energy field, hands-on, hands-off or at a distance. Reiki, therapeutic touch, qigong and crystal healing are typical examples.

In appearance culture, its pull is relaxation and stress reduction, which practitioners connect to skin, sleep and general glow. Research reviews, however, have not found clinical efficacy for energy healing.
quick.how: Sessions are usually a practitioner holding hands near or on the body, or distance healing. Some people use qigong self-practice. It is generally used alongside everyday care.
quick.risks: The main documented harm is delaying or forgoing medical treatment. Some device sellers have been prosecuted by the FDA for false claims.

lead: Energy medicine is a branch of alternative medicine built on the belief that healers can direct healing energy into patients. Wikipedia describes it as pseudoscientific and notes the concept is unrelated to the physical concept of energy [1]. Practitioners work hands-on, hands-off or at a distance [1].

Main forms include biofield healing, therapeutic touch, Reiki, qigong, crystal healing and Pranic Healing [1]. The US National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health divides the field into veritable energy medicine (measurable energies like magnets and light) and putative energy medicine (energies that cannot be measured, such as Reiki) [1].

Proponents hold that illness reflects imbalance in the body's energy field and that rebalancing restores wellbeing [1]. Appearance claims are secondary: advocates link relaxation and lower stress to better skin, sleep and looks.

chain: Sleep and skin often tied to stress
angle.text: Users seek relaxation and stress relief, which some connect to better sleep and fresher-looking skin. The link to appearance is a belief held by practitioners, not an outcome tested in trials.

paras: In the 19th century, electricity and magnetism spread widely as health claims, and in the early 20th century radioactive materials were marketed similarly. The International Society for the Study of Subtle Energies and Energy Medicine was founded in the 1980s, bioresonance therapy was invented in Germany in 1977 by Franz Morell and Erich Rasche, and in 2005-2006 the North American Nursing Diagnosis Association approved an 'energy field disturbance' diagnosis, which has been criticized [1].

Some proponents have invoked quantum non-locality or bioelectromagnetism to explain distant healing, which critics call pseudophysics [1]. One review defined the biofield as including nonclassical and quantum energy fields [3].

A 2000 systematic review of 23 distant-healing trials was inconclusive due to methodological problems, and a 2001 randomized trial of 120 chronic pain patients found no efficacy for either distance or face-to-face healing. Edzard Ernst concluded in 2003 and 2006 that evidence had turned negative, and a 2014 trial in colorectal cancer patients showed no improvement in quality of life, depression, mood or sleep [1].

A randomized double-blind trial of Spiritist 'passe' healing in preterm newborns examined stress hormone, pain and length of stay [2]. A review of pilot studies with cultured cells tested whether practitioners could perceive a biofield [4].

Reliance on energy healing has been linked to serious harm or death when patients delay medical treatment. The FDA classifies devices that diagnose and treat disease by resistance measurements as Class III, has banned some, and has prosecuted sellers for false claims [1]. Reported improvements are generally attributed to placebo effects, spontaneous remission and research flaws [1].
